extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on managing point of view and the twin methods of 'picture' (pictorial narration/omniscient chronicle) and 'drama' (scenic enactment) in the novel, including when to use first person and how to dramatize the narrator. Focuses on achieving authenticity, unity, and intensity in long fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture vs. Drama (two fundamental methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between the pictorial method (a reflected picture of life, panoramic, chronicle-like) and the dramatic method (close, scenic enactment where the story 'appears to tell itself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture: 'the story passes into Thackeray's book as a picture' — broad, discursive, allows large extents of life to be represented but tends to introduce the omniscient author. Drama: 'in Maupassant's drama we are close to the facts... the story appears to tell itself' — immediate, intense, scene-driven. A novelist typically prefers one method but must manage and combine both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve drama for essential occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is 'the novelist's highest light' and should not be used prodigally; it should be hoarded for important occasions where intensity is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenic enactment sparingly — "to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential." The economical procedure is to 'hoard it rather, reserving it for important occasions — as in Bovary.' Overuse wastes dramatic value and diminishes climactic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the point of view / 'dramatize the seeing eye'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the authorial mind and eye that 'knows the story' are unaccountable, the novelist should make that point of view an objective, verifiable fact within the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrator's knowledge remains unexplained, the book may feel unfinished or have "a loose end." The only way to silence questions about the narrator's authority is 'to make the mind and the eye objective, to make them facts in the story.' Techniques to do this will be discussed (e.g., narrator in character, first person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conspicuous omniscient narration without authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: An omniscient author who is too conspicuous risks drawing the reader's attention away from the book and creating an inconclusive look; the narrator's relation to the story must be accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thackeray's method, in which the point of view is obviously the author's ('the point of view is his — not to be confounded with that of anybody in the book'), can make a book seem 'not really self-contained' and create 'an inconclusive look' that pulls the reader out of the fiction. Prudence is advised in using omniscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the narrator a character ('narrator in character')
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn the recorder/authorial consciousness into a directly perceptible actor in the book (a 'drama of the narrator'), so the relation of seer to seen is shown and testable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Esmond — the narrator stands among the people he describes, so his 'line of sight' is measureable and Beatrix gains 'a new dimension and a sharper relief.' Thackeray later 'refused to remain the unaccountable seer' by making his narrator dramatized, though sometimes used loosely. This device authenticates and heightens reported impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person to give precision, individuality, and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting a characterized 'I' (a named, particular narrator) for the author's general 'I' bounds the field of vision, supplies tone, and can unify a rambling or discursive design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: the picture gains a 'definite edge,' 'precision, individuality,' 'the comfortable assurance of the point of view,' and personal colour. It 'composes of its own accord' and can 'draw a rambling, fragmentary tale together' (e.g., David Copperfield, Harry Richmond). Caution: first person can also disguise formlessness and has 'snares' if used to mask weak structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose first person when the subject suits autobiography-like vision
rubrics_metrics.description: When the novel's shape depends on a span of memory or the subject is the speaker's experience, first person is especially appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: David Copperfield — a long glance over years where the past shapes the book; Harry Richmond — adventures tied to a particular young man's life. In such cases the 'hero gives the story an indefeasible unity by the mere act of telling it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend methods: impose one method upon another to correct weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist should 'impose method upon method' — use dramatization to strengthen the pictorial/chronicling passages so as to retain advantages of both picture and drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is 'that everything in the novel, not only the scenic episodes but all the rest, is to be in some sense dramatized.' Good novelists 'correct the weakness of one method by the force of another' and thereby avoid the chief defects of each when used alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that narration sacrifices intensity without dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial narration gives freedom and range but pays for it by loss of intensity unless the narrational material is dramatized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The freedom of the pictorial method 'has to be paid for by some loss of intensity,' and the question is how to 'pay as little as possible.' The solution proposed is to dramatize elements of the chronicle so that the loss is made good and the novel retains both breadth and concentrated force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use point of view deliberately to determine what the reader can test
rubrics_metrics.description: Information presented solely as the narrator's report lacks weight unless it can be tested or verified by material in the book; dramatizing viewpoint gives that verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turgenev's fiction, where the narrator frequently 'draws the reader aside and pours into his ear a flow of information... which will never have its due weight' because the reader cannot test it, is given as a caution. Make the narrator's knowledge derive from perceivable action or placed perspective so the reader can accept it.
